title: Many streams
hookLine: the panth holds many orders and schools, each with its own emphasis

lines: A MAN IN DEEP BLUE AT THE DOOR.
A QUIET MAN AT THE POTS.
cards: A big city gurdwara on a holiday morning. Near the door stands a man in deep blue, his turban wound high and ringed with steel.

Inside, a young student reads from the Granth slowly, every syllable placed like a stone in a wall. In the kitchen, an older man in plain white washes pots. Upstairs, a group has been singing since before dawn.

They all bowed to the same Granth on the way in. They didn't all learn their ways in the same place. After weeks with the code that holds the panth together, today we start meeting the streams that run inside it.

teach.b: The word for a stream like that is sampardaa: a tradition handed on, teacher to student, with its own way of doing things. Over the coming weeks you'll meet several. Some are orders of renunciants who look after shrines.
Some are scholars who wrote commentaries. One is known for quiet service, one keeps the old martial life on horseback, one teaches careful recitation, one sings through the night.
Each puts its weight on a different thing, and each, in its own telling, traces its line back to the Gurus.
In the hymn Sikhs call Sohila, sung at night, Guru Nanak speaks of six schools, six teachers and six teachings. Then, in paraphrase: but the Teacher of teachers is one, appearing in many forms.

He was speaking about the schools of his own day, not about Sikh orders that came later. Still, the shape of the thought helps: many ways of teaching, one source. Two honest things belong next to that.

First, Sikhs hold a range of views about these streams: how close each stands to the Khalsa's code, where an emphasis becomes a difference. Some of those questions are still argued, and this path won't settle them.

teach.h: A STREAM IS NOT A WALL.
teach.b: Second, a stream is not a wall.

A Sikh can learn kirtan from one, pronunciation from another, and service from a third, and come home to the same congregation. So meet each one on its own terms, hear what it cares about most, and rank none of them.

how: Sikhs learn from more than one sampardaa: a congregation may hear kirtan in one style, katha from a scholar of another school, and recitation taught by a third, while all bow to the Guru Granth Sahib.

a teaching line handed on, teacher to student
a festival shared by every Sikh community

games.q: Guru Nanak names six schools, six teachers and six teachings. what does he say next?
o: that one of the six is right and the rest are wrong.
that the Teacher of teachers is one, in many forms.
that teachers aren't needed at all.
games.why: the Teacher of teachers is one, appearing in many forms. many ways of teaching; one source.

practice: From the streams you heard about today, the shrine keepers, the scholars, the servers, the riders, the readers, the night singers, choose the one you know least about and hold just its outline in mind, without judging it.
Breathe in with the question, what does this one care about most, and breathe out leaving the answer open.

wordCard.voice: Sampardaa. A tradition handed on from teacher to student, with its own emphasis. The panth holds several, and each traces itself to the Gurus. Today's word.

orig.note: Punjabi: a tradition or school handed down from teacher to student.

carryVoice: Your line: many streams, one guru. Each one gets its own day. See you tomorrow.
